passage:
On the last Friday of the month, with the electricity bill due by five and Papa's clinic visit the next morning, Gurleen stood in the bank queue doing sums and stewing. For two years she had done the paperwork, the pharmacy runs and the phone calls to relatives. Nilesh sent money and "good luck" messages. She had been keeping score in silence, and today it sat like a lump in her chest.

When the queue cleared she called him instead of texting. "Nilesh, I'm not angry, I'm tired. I do nearly everything for Papa and Mummy. Can we sit down on Sunday and divide it?"

He was silent. "I thought you liked being in charge. I'm sorry. I can take the clinic runs and the bills online."

"I'd like that," Gurleen said. She paid the bill with two minutes to spare.

qa.q: When was the electricity bill due?
qa.a: By five, on the last Friday of the month.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling as she waited in the bank queue?
qa.a: Tired and resentful. She had been keeping score in silence for two years and it sat like a lump in her chest.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do to avoid an explosion?
qa.a: She called Nilesh, spoke honestly without anger, and proposed sitting down on Sunday to divide the tasks.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have seen the arrangement before the call?
qa.a: He assumed Gurleen liked being in charge. His apology and offer suggest he hadn't realised how much she carried.

grounding: One sibling handles the ageing parents' errands and money more than the other; Gurleen has an honest conversation about fair shares under time pressure.

Sangeeta: binu, can we talk about amma-appa? properly
Binita: sure, what happened?? 😟
Sangeeta: nothing new. that's the problem. i've done every hospital visit this year. 7 of them
Sangeeta: and i've been counting silently and getting angry at you, which isn't fair since i never said anything
Binita: oh. i didn't realise it was 7
Binita: i've been feeling guilty but from pune i just... didn't know how to help
Sangeeta: ok. can we split it? you could handle the medicine orders and insurance online. and come home for the next visit in june
Binita: yes. and i'll call appa every evening so you don't have to do that too
Sangeeta: that would help a lot
Binita: thanks for telling me before you exploded 😅
Sangeeta: i was close
Binita: i know. i'm sorry. june's booked

qa.q: How many hospital visits had Sangeeta done this year?
How had Sangeeta been feeling about the visits?
qa.a: Angry and resentful, counting silently, while knowing it wasn't fair since Sangeeta had never said anything.

qa.q: What split did Sangeeta and Binita agree on?
qa.a: Binita handles medicine orders and insurance online, calls Appa every evening, and comes home for the June visit.

qa.q: How had Binita felt from Pune?
qa.a: Guilty but unsure how to help, and unaware that it had been seven visits.

grounding: Shows one sibling carrying most of the care of ageing parents, and having an honest talk about fair shares before silent score-keeping explodes.

passage:
In their village outside Dharwad, Hemant had run the family's small grocery and looked after their parents for three years while his sister Bhavna studied in Bengaluru. He never complained. He just kept a list in his head: every doctor trip, every bill, every night Appa couldn't sleep.
At Diwali, when Bhavna arrived with gifts and said, "Amma looks so well!", the list came out all at once. "Of course she does. I'm the one who takes her everywhere! You come twice a year with sweets!"
Bhavna went white. Amma started crying. Hemant walked out to the fields, hands shaking.
An hour later Bhavna found him by the well. "I didn't know. You never said."
"I know." He rubbed his face. "I should have told you in March, not shouted at Diwali."
They sat on the edge of the well and made a plan: Bhavna would pay the pharmacy bill each month and come home one weekend a month; Hemant would call her first whenever something happened. It wasn't perfectly equal. But it was said.

qa.q: For how long had Hemant looked after their parents?
What made Hemant's hands shake as he walked to the fields?
qa.a: Anger that had built up silently for three years, and then shame at having shouted in front of Amma.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Hemant kept score silently until it exploded; an honest talk by the well led to a plan: Bhavna pays the pharmacy bill and visits monthly, and Hemant calls her first.

qa.q: How did Bhavna experience the Diwali outburst?
qa.a: Shocked and hurt, because she had not known; Hemant had never said anything.

grounding: Illustrates silent score-keeping over family duties exploding, and then an honest conversation about fair shares between siblings.
